questions.prompt: Why does a POMDP planner use a belief state instead of the latest observation?
options: A belief removes the need for any sensor model, since it is learned directly from rewards
Observations are never available during planning, so the planner must guess the state
The belief is always deterministic, so the planner can treat the state as exactly known
The belief summarises the history and the uncertainty, while the last observation can be wrong
questions.explanation: The belief is a sufficient statistic of history; the last observation ignores noise and past evidence.

questions.prompt: Tiger problem: b = P(tiger left) = 0.5, sensor accuracy 0.85. Posterior after hearing 'left'? (3 decimals)
b = 0.7, accuracy 0.85. Probability of hearing 'left'? (3 decimals)
Opening the right door gives +10 if the tiger is left and -100 otherwise. At b = 0.9 (tiger left), expected reward of opening the right door?
When is a clarifying measurement NOT worth taking?
options: When the sensor is noisy, since a noisy reading can never change the belief at all
Whenever the planning horizon is long, because early information is always forgotten later
When no possible outcome would change the chosen action, or its cost exceeds the expected gain
When the belief is uniform, because there is nothing left that a measurement could tell us
questions.explanation: Information is valuable only through the decisions it changes, net of cost.

questions.prompt: Acting now at b=0.5 gives -45; one listen (cost 1) leads to a belief where the best action is worth -6.5 in both cases. Value of listening once?
A sensor with accuracy 0.5 (pure coin flips) is used before acting. The best policy is:
options: Treat the reading as the true state and act on it without updating
Ignore it: the posterior equals the prior and sensing only costs
Trust it fully, since any reading is better than acting on the prior alone
Use it twice, so that the two coin flips average out to a reliable signal

questions.prompt: A manipulator is unsure whether an object is a cup or a bottle (80 percent cup). Grasping wrongly breaks something; a second camera view costs 1 second. Describe how you would decide between grasping now and taking the view, including the quantities you need and how you would validate the decision.
rubric: Define rewards for correct/incorrect grasps and the cost of the view.
Update the belief with the camera's accuracy for each outcome and compare expected values.
Validate on logged data or simulation using the hidden class, and test a sensor of accuracy 0.5 as a boundary case.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
